title: Inside Star Citizen: Dev Diary: Gavin Rothery

segments.text: It's no secret that Star Citizen is an ambitious game,
trying to build a first-person universe of varied experiences across multiple star systems.
But at its core will always be the spaceship.
And the process of making a spaceship always begins with a concept artist.
We've had no shortage of greats contribute to our legacy of vehicles.
From Star Wars superstars like Ryan Church and David Hobbins,
to Star Trek luminaries like Jim Martin.
From the art departments of Godzilla, Matrix, Blade Runner and Dune like Emmanuel Shui and George Hull,
to the dedicated CIG legends like Paul Jones and Alberto Petronio,
and a whole host of folks in between two numerous dimensions,
the origin of our spacecraft are as numerous as their manufacturers.
But there's one person who's participated in the birth of more Star Citizen spacecraft than any other.
With more than 20 vehicles to his name so far,
he bridges the gaps between manufacturers and has helped to define or refine many of their styles over the years.
And this year's special ship showdown showcase,
we brought the prolific Gavin Rothery into our office for your chance to meet the man
and celebrate just a fraction of his contribution to this project.
And because I just think he's neat.
Let's go.
I'm not toothpaste all I've got.
You're a toothpaste fly.
I think working as a concept artist is great.
I like the way I get to spend time with my dogs.
I really appreciate that.
I've got my dogs around me all day.
I get my special ships, my dogs, you know,
and I get to come up to Manchester and hang out with you guys for a bit.
It's awesome.
What do you get?
You use toothpaste once.
Beautiful.
Oh, I'll do.
That's right.
I'm an artist.
So a concept artist is usually a human.
That might change.
We've seen these AIs.
They're coming for us.
So a concept artist is an artist who comes in at the start of a job
and works through a technical brief, which is often just writing.
There might be a few reference images in there.
Occasionally, we don't really tend to work like that.
We'll just get a technical brief and you've got to come down.
You've got to realise things.
Usually you're working in somewhat in isolation.
There's base touching with art directors and such.
But like a lot of my job is me just working at home in my studio.
Just kind of getting on with things, having like regular touchings.
And that sounds weird.
Touching base frequently.
And just pushing the design forward, basically.
So I'm given a brief and a deadline
and I'm expected to metamorphosise that brief
into something that can fulfil that brief
and look really cool on the clock.
There's a few things that make a good concept artist really.
You've got to be able to get along with people
and like fit into a team.
That's first and foremost because it's more remote
so it can take longer to get relationships going with people.
So that stuff becomes more important.
Again, project particularly, there's lots of things changing in development.
So you've got to be able to approach your work with a mindset of like
not being too precious about it.
You can do a bunch of work on things and it can all be beautiful.
And that could just completely change
and you have to do something else which is beautiful.
You've got to just be able to wake up every morning
and kind of deliver that.
Whenever you see a good concept artist,
you'll be looking at somebody that is able to do that
and figure it out in their life.
So Star Citizen is a very unique beast.
I've been in the games industry for a long time.
I've worked in movies.
I've been around the block, I've done stuff.
Star Citizen is one of those projects that's got such
definitively harsh metrics that you need to fit
that I've never worked on another project like it.
You can look at the Millennium Falcon,
you know, it looks pretty on the outside,
it looks pretty on the inside.
Those two things don't go together.
So with Star Citizen, everything has to fit.
And I remember when I first started doing some of the bigger ships
like many years ago, that was a new thing to me
because other projects don't really consider that.
They'll have, once you're inside a ship,
you're basically inside a magic little universe
and, you know, things can be completely different scales
and people generally don't worry about that stuff too much.
With Star Citizen, it's all cohesive and it all has to fit.
And so when we're designing it, we'll start with the exterior.
We always do options for things.
So the first week of a new ship design is me doing,
like, just blasting out options as quickly as I can.
When I'm designing a ship, I work in 3D and 2D.
So my actual pipeline is I do all my 3D in Maya,
so I get the brief, I just go straight into 3D
and just start blocking out ships and basically sketching in 3D.
I've been doing this for a long time as a concept artist
and I've found that working in ships and volume,
it's just a very natural way to work.
It's a sculptural medium.
I always just get straight into 3D
and I don't really work from one angle to start off
without literally working with the 3D shape

So I work my way in from blocking 3D shapes.
So this is all done in Maya.
And I like to put four, five options together

There'll be a range of things in there.
Try and make them all quite different.
Quite often you'll have a favorite,

title: Star Citizen | Behind the Ships: Argo MOTH

segments.text: The Argo Moth is the long-awaited, much-requested medium salvager for star citizen.
It's supposed to fill the gaps between our small single-seed salvage ships,
such as the Vulture and the Salvation, and the massive Aegis Reclaimer.
Small salvage ships, they produce rubble.
The large one, like the Reclaimer, they produce construction material salvage.
And the medium ship, we create construction material pieces.
The refining time for the rubble is the fastest for the pieces.
It's like in the medium park, whereas for the salvage,
it's like the longest refining time that we'll take.
For crafting, the difference between the three different
construction material raw versions of it will be that the...
basically retaining the quality of the material.
With the Moth, we wanted to take our medium operator-sized ships that we have already.
We have the Moth. It's a great ship.
And pivot that system over into salvage.
Sometimes you don't need to reinvent the wheel,
and we thought that building on top of the Moth to make the Moth made perfect sense.
The Moth is successful as a mining ship, particularly multi-crew wise,
due to the fact that it has all those turrets that can cover pretty much
the entire 360 degrees under the ship, as well as around it.
It's not completely full coverage, but it's pretty good.
And the turrets have freedom of movement to really mine anywhere.
And that really lends itself to salvage as well,
which shares a lot of that sort of similar mechanics.
I think the Moth is a very successful ship in what it's built for.
So getting the opportunity to revisit it with the lessons we've learned
and put some new life into it with a slightly different role
and slightly different purpose, really exciting.
And this allows us to iterate more easily on our current ships that are going out.
But it also means that we can take some of those improvements and changes
back to those original ships later down the line.
We've tried to make changes where they were needed,
but not make changes for changes' sake.
But the kind of like the standout thing, if I'm honest, is the arms.
What's your favorite aspect of the Moth?
My favorite aspect is the new grinders.
The giant munching arms that it's got on the front, they look great.
They just feel kind of super chunky, super industrial, super dangerous.
My favorite aspect of the ship is the grabbing hands.
They look really cool and give it a nice quirk to the ship.
Probably the grabbing hands.
Group is just grabbing hands, why?
It is such a key part of the ship's visuals,
because they're very big, very industrial.
There's lots of weight behind them,
but at the same time there's also really intricate little details.
I was trying to make them look a bit intimidating,
like a bit dangerous, like you really wouldn't want your hands to be caught in anything.
It was also very fun to work on the animations,
to kind of figure out how in the different states the arms would kind of retract,
the claws would open up, big hydraulic pistons kind of retracting, moving around.
And yeah, of course the crushers spinning.
Are you aware that nearly a decade ago we had another system called Grabby Hands
that has nothing to do with this?
No, I was not aware. What was that?
Disco Lino remembers.
It takes a crew of four, so far fewer than you need for the Reclaimer.
But it actually gives you some multiplayer gameplay as opposed to the Vulture.
All four of those players will be able to take part in the salvage gameplay loop.
We have three manned turrets, each with a size two salvage head,
and the pilot gets access to the main structural salvage crusher.
Can this ship be operated solo?
Yeah, like all our ships it can be operated solo,
but if you operate a ship solo of a certain size, you get some downsides to it.
It would just be a lot of dancing around between the different seats,
but at the same time you're also going to be saving some time because you're going to be able
to carry a lot more. So you're going to have less ships back and forth.
What kind of defensive capabilities does this thing have?
Very minimal defensive capabilities. This is first and foremost an industrial ship.
The pilot has two S2 slots available to them.
The co-pilot gets access to a bespoke small missile rack with 16 S2 missiles.
The belly of the ship has changed quite a lot.
We've now got this large split cargo grid that is in a vertical orientation.
So when the salvage material is ejected out,
it blows straight onto this large cargo grid that kind of takes up the majority of the belly of the ship.
One of the improvements over the mole chassis is the fact that the cargo
grids are just normal cargo grids. Whilst the salvage output does automatically eject onto them,
and it does use standardised ASU crates, there's nothing to stop you putting any other cargo
compatible item on those cargo grids, which allows you to then perhaps do a bit of cargo.
Maybe you find some salvage on the way that you want to do.
It doesn't limit you to doing one or the other.
You do have the ability to do both at the same time.
The rear of the ship has a really nice cargo lift for two 16 SCU crates.
You can get a bit of hauling gameplay in there as well.
And just in front of that is the old personnel lift.
Both take you up into the newly sort of slightly reimagined cargo area.
From there to the left and right, you've got the entrances to the side salvage turrets.
And then a ladder that leaves you up onto the main deck.
One of the things we realised as we were working on the ship was to be able to get out some of the
components out of the ship. We needed to widen the doors and widen the ladder down to the lower
floor and this gives a nice route through the ship to be able to get those ship items out.
To the rear of the ship from there are the beds and the bathroom and a couple of suit lockers.
And then forwards from habitation is into the processing room.
We basically took the pre-existent engineering room from the mall and converted to a processing room.
It feels very hot, very industrial and a little claustrophobic.
You have an engineering screen in the middle. Some of the components have been sort of reshuffled around
to make space for a big refinery which is on board.
Forward further still is the bridge which has the pilot and copilot seats.
As we're kind of revisiting the cockpit, we've updated it a little bit.
We've brought in a few new interactions, kind of modernised the view a little bit.
Things like the dashboard improvements, the interactive panels that we placed around the ship,
those sort of things will kind of be retrofitted back onto the mall as well.
Like the Asgard and the Hermes, the moth is a new hull based on an existing chassis and that
means it doesn't share paints with the mall. But we are making some really nice new paints for the moth.
So we're going to have a lot of two-tone paints coming in.
So you'll see that we have decided to spice them up a bit.
So we're excited now that we have the full set of salvage ship sizes.
We have you starting with the salvation, moving to the vulture and fortune.
Now we have the moth and then ultimately you end up with the reclaimer.
It was very fun to work on, very nice to work on something industrial.
Just the little changes to the flow that we've had to make,
opening up some areas just to allow a little bit of a smoother kind of gameplay experience has been really nice.
This is for the person who enjoys salvage gameplay but wants something bigger.

segments.text: Starterships are important because they are the entryway into a career that you may not necessarily have thought you want to play.

Starterships are also important to have a sense of progression through the ship lineup.

We're proud to introduce the entry-level salvage ship, the RSI Salvation.
The RSI Salvation is a new salvage starter from the manufacturer RSI.
It's the first ship off the production line for that profession in the game.
The salvation is for those players who want to get into the salvage career or those who have sort of been curious about it but wanted an easy way into that loop.
This allows you to access the new RMC and salvage changes very easily.
The RSI Salvation is a beautiful, compact solo ship.

We wanted it to look strong but quite stubby.
It was a balance between making it feel industrial, feel functional and strong.
So when you first look at it, the first thing you're going to notice is these structural elements that are like an external roll cage that wrap around either side of the ship.

On either side we've got these fins that open up so when you go into salvage mode there's like somewhere for it to like release its energy, release its heat that it's not needing.

You deploy your salvage arms and they're just partly the side of you.

So there are six principles for good level design.
First is readability. This basically means clarity in your environment.
You're going to make sure within your layouts that everybody can understand where they need to go, what they need to do.
All the affordances need to make sense. The typical one could be, I've got a door in front of me.
How do you describe a locked door from an unlocked door?
For example, you're fighting an AI and they can read easily the elements, the gameplay elements.
You need to understand your cover space. You need to find the AI within the space.
If the AI is in a black area, you will not see it at all.
And this is very important for us. We really focus on this kind of stuff and we make sure that anything you interact with within the environment,
you can see as clear as possible.
Next is flow and leading lines.
It's creating a good composition of all these things from layout, lighting, some props,
a good mix of combat spaces or combat encounters and then time for exploration and then doing a mix between both.
We make sure that you're not going always on a straight line.
We make sure that you're not spending two hours walking from one space to the other.
In Pyro, you'll come across a lot more players as we funnel them into a certain space.
With the concentration of missions, for example, or things to do, that is flow to us on the flow level, that is higher on the chart.
And then certain errors will be a bit more on the lower end of your pacing.
Leading lines is a compositional technique.
Some examples can be you are following the cables from one interactable through to another arrow to interact with another element.
You're being breadacrumbed along, you're being led along these leading lines.
With Pyro's station, you have the core element, you have the arms pointing towards the center.
It's a very simple example, but more on a larger scale, but we look at it also on a room basis.
We're trying to direct you through to a discoverable place over here or trying to direct you through to an event.
We're using lights and cables to navigate you through these spaces.
Pyro is options. We want to give you guys multiple options so you can complete your objective the way you want it.
The context of our game is giving the player the opportunity to approach certain situations in different ways or get an idea of the situation in the first place.
You have late-forward options, the combat route, you have a more sneaky option for players that don't like to engage in combat so much,
or you can also have like a puzzle route for players that like to do more interesting environment interactions.
Then there is clustering.
Clustering also falls into compositional techniques or more in the layout side of things.
Clustering means that you start bringing objects together to create something a bit more natural.
You put importance on things by grouping certain things up into clusters.

we're taking a renewed effort to concentrate and cluster things properly.

This is the original design direction that we wanted from beginning through to end.
Once a location is released it's not finished for us because there is always maintenance and additions that we do.

Level design matters always important because we think of a very broad scale and try to craft and create a great experience for you as a player.
Level design ends up being greater than the sum of all of its parts.
I get to talk with all these different disciplines at CIG, but also get to kind of like hold the hand of the player and curate that all the way through.
We focus on the player experience.
We look at all the features that exist and we try to bring them up all together into a cohesive environment.
That feels really fun for the players.
Do you always succeed?
No, but it's not always like within our hands, but we always try our best to within the framework we have to create like the best possible experience for you guys.
So we've learned a lot from our time in Stanton and we love hearing what the feedback we get from you as players.
We want to take the all on board and begin establishing ourselves forwards when we come into Pyro.
What we really want to do also is balance out gameplay with the visuals.
I mean in the past we've seen a lot of focus being spent on the visuals and less on the content.
This needs to switch around and find an even plane and level design is just one way we're doing this in Pyro.
We as level designers really want to make Pyro and stand in the future great experience for the players from a flow perspective.
Boring you less, making things more efficient for you as you follow the gameplay loops that you want to follow and offer you gameplay content that you can just discover on your own.
So what we learned this week?

what we always hope is a cohesive and enjoyable experience for the player.

And that Pyro itself continues to inspire an experience that should be markedly different from the one we have today in Stanton.
For Inside Star Citizen, I'm Jared Huckabee.
Thanks for letting us share the people and process of game development with you and we'll see you all here next week.

title: Star Citizen | Behind the Ships: Esperia Prowler Utility

segments.text: The Prowler Utility is a brand new dedicated cargo ship with enhanced stealth abilities.
It trades some of its combat capabilities for more industrial uses.
If you don't want to get detected during your cargo run, this is the perfect ship.
This ship is for someone who wants to do cargo,
wants to remain stealthy, and who wants to look sick by doing it.
The Prowler Utility is different from the baseline Prowler.
Because we had to carve out extra space for the new cargo, that meant that the belly section
of the ship had to increase in size just a tiny bit.
It also has a ventral size-to-remote tractor beam, which can be accessed from the pilot or
copilot seat. And that will allow you to move cargo freely in and out of the ship.
The base version of the ship has these feathers on the wings, which get deployed down when you land,
but those are no longer really needed since the functionality is slightly different.
And so what we've done now is when you land with this ship, those feathers get tucked up,
giving you more space to actually move cargo around the ship freely.
It features two size-four guns under the wings instead of the original two size-five guns,
while retaining the remote turret on top with the two size-three weapons.
As the Prowler Utility is a variant of the Prowler, rather than the standalone chassis,
it gets to share all the cool paints between both versions.
And existing Prowler owners of course get to benefit from all the new paints that come with the launch of this vehicle.
We've updated the lighting quite a bit in order to sort of just give a little more feedback to the player.
We've chosen to really lead me into sort of the red lighting that we've been doing on the interior of the Prowler in general,
and pushed that to the exterior.
And so if you're coming down above someone, you just look like this incredibly aggressive silhouette with red lights flashing everywhere.
I think it looks awesome.
Compared to the base Prowler, we have stripped out the lower interior by removing the main side of the hull.
We've removed the main section of drop seats and replacing that with a 32 SCU cargo hull.
And added a sort of clam shell door opening on the undersides to allow easy access to the cargo bay.
It essentially looks like a facehugger, but a facehugger cargo.
There's a new engineering room on the upper deck, which is previously where a component closet was.
And it retains three of the four jump seats up front in the co-pilot foyer,
and replaces one of those drop seats with a storage rack for handheld cargo boxes.
I'm super happy with how it turned out, and I'm excited to see the feedback from players and how they end up using it in the game.
We wanted to try and come up with an arrangement of the cargo hold and the tractor beam in such a way that you could potentially swoop in

segments.text: There's a lot of gameplay loops in Star Citizen.
There's mining, salvage, cargo, piracy, and a whole host of combat roles
ranging from large capital ships which require a huge crew
down to the single player fighters with more coming online over the next year.
There's a lot of players that specialize in each of those roles and there's
ships that are dedicated to those roles. But there's also a lot of players that
sort of don't want to be put in a box and they just want to leave themselves open
to whatever happens in the verse. We refer to this as the generalist playstyle.
We have a few ships that sort of fit into that role such as the Cutter and the Corsair.
We felt there was an ideal space in the middle to introduce a new ship
and that's the Drake Clipper. The Drake Clipper is the jack of all trades, the master of none, really.
So it's the jury of the spaceship. It is Drake's answer to the ship that does a little bit of everything
and it's really there for the person that wants to go out, explore,
but without needing to bring along friends. It is Drake's solo ship for the person that
just wants to go and see what the universe has to offer. The Clipper is that silhouette that
everyone has been hankering for, for instance, in Conn 2024, the large vertical multi-positioned wing
Drake ship. We had a few different ideas that we tried and we ended with one that was very thin
and narrow that CR quite liked and we saw it as like a stepping point between the Cutter and the
Corsair as like the middle ground between those. It just looked straight, you looked at it and you know.

copied late to the work? Oh 100% yeah. From the outside I think the first thing you kind of
notice when you walk up to it is just how tall it is. The role we wanted it to have,
we wanted it to be able to do loads of different stuff but we wanted to keep it within a really
small solo footprint and so what we decided to do was build on its height. I love it's like top

That's always an immersion breaker when you see giant shoulder pads clipping through people's heads and stuff like that.
Well, so what we do for, since everything that we make is built off, like Josh was saying, a base character
that might blend in between 50 other characters, which in this example could be 50 different t-shirts.
So in order to kind of prevent that, you really have to take the base mail that we use for our game
and match whatever assets or clothing that we have on top of them,
and kind of match it as close to possible one-to-one with what's underneath it,
because the male body will always be there, or the female body will always be underneath the armor or the clothing or whatever.
So you really have to build or create enough polygons or density in your assets to kind of like prevent anything from clipping.
Because usually when that happens, it's because you don't have enough topology or polygons in your clothing to kind of support what's underneath it.
So to really, I mean, prevent that with like modern games now, you can add so many polygons.
So it's really just a matter of like supporting whatever's on top of your base model to kind of follow the underlying structure of your model to kind of prevent that from happening.
And then on top of that, we're also looking, we have a basic way to do it now, but we're looking into like a much larger cloth, Sam.
So right now you can take a coat and it'll kind of dangle and when it moves around, it'll kind of basically stuff that.

We've also been looking into, hoping, but you know, crossing our fingers for wrinkle maps.
Like there's a lot of games that you'll see like when somebody like lifts up their shirt or then they twist, like the wrinkles in your shirt change completely.
Whereas when you're just doing, you know, the old, old Jane of Games would have the same wrinkles, but when they would bend, it would just kind of like twist into this weird shape.

I don't know, put a cart? Was he the god of goods?
Hermes was the herald of the gods and considered the protector of the human heralds,
so responsible for people travelling from one location to another and moving things around.
Perfect.
The Hermes is RSI's first dedicated medium freighter.
We were discussing new ships quite some time ago and at that point we were developing the Apollo
and the Hermes seemed a natural chassis alteration for the Apollo series.
With the RSI Apollo it was received very well in terms of its styling
and really what we wanted to do was take those visuals and just make it available for a new audience.
The main distinguishing feature of the Hermes is it has much larger beefed up thrusters visually on the outside.
It needs a lot of power to move that way around.
One of the things we wanted to try and convey with its visuals was this idea that it had a lot more strength than what the base Apollo did.
So if you look at the very top of the ship you'll notice that where there's a big window in the Apollo
you're seeing much more of the inner structure of the ship,
so it's reinforced with large girders and these big metal plates that make it feel a lot stronger.
Whilst its official designation is a medium freighter, the Hermes is sort of internally often referred to as a sort of blockade runner.
It's great performance in a straight line with those extra beefy thrusters.
It has some good armour, obviously the weapons are all upgraded compared to the Apollo series.
It has 16 S2 missiles.
It can pack a punch while providing very competitive SCM and nav speeds at the expense of some manoeuvrability.
Inside the front half of the ship shares virtually everything with the Apollo series
and that is your bridge and habs and component room, but the back half is a completely different story.
It's pretty obvious that things have changed.
It basically strips out any of the interior that isn't essential to the ship's flight
and replaces it with a large cargo space.
Capable of holding 288 SEU and that includes being able to hold the 32 SEU crates.
There isn't a lot of ships in that 200 to 300 SEU cargo range.
You have the RAF series that's down at 192 and then you have sort of the Caterpillar series that is 500 plus.
There isn't really many ships in that middle zone.
The whole B is moving up to 512, that was sort of the closest.
But of course the Hermes carries all of its cargo internally compared to say the whole series which has it all external and much more vulnerable.
One of the things we realised when we were developing the ship was having a cargo space that is quite short but very wide
and then trying to bring the cargo into the space was quite difficult.
So a design team came up with this idea of having this tractor beam that ran on a rail through the centre of the cargo space.
And that really allows you to be able to hold that cargo in quite easily.
And the tractor beam can be controlled from either the copilot seat or a dedicated station at the rear of the ship.
So if you've ever had problems playing cargo Tetris then the Hermes might be the ship for you.
So in terms of paints on the Hermes, the default paint is kind of a nod back to the Zouciel.
So you have another cargo ship from RSI.
We thought it would be nice to continue that theme and that brand recognition across the cargo ships on the RSI line up.
The Apollo was quite a serious ship so for the paints for the Hermes we thought we'd have a bit more fun.
We've got a nice two-tone black and yellow.
We've got a purple and yellow and white.
And because Jared cries when we don't and he's quite persistent at coming and appearing at my desk,
we also did the disco paint that we did for the RSI meteor.
So again it builds on that brand recognition and it keeps Jared happy.
This ship is obviously for those focused on cargo hauling.
But you can also fit quite a lot of our smaller ground vehicles in there.
So it's a great little ship to reposition things around.
A lot of people have said that they love the Apollo's look but don't like the medical gameplay.
So this really is the ship for those people.
It's fast, sleek and it's very just versatile ships so I think people are going to enjoy it.

title: Star Citizen | Behind the Ships: Argo ATLS GEO

segments.text: The Atlas is a power suit that assists players loading cargo into their ship with a tractor beam.
So it's supposed to work as a cargo carrier in your personal hangar to move giant boxes around.
Now we are introducing the Atlas Geo and that is a mining mac.
The Geo's beam is a vehicle mining beam.
But with the press of a button you can reduce the power to fit the expected power of an FPS mineable.
The Geo does not have the regular tractor beam, it only comes with the mining arm and the mining laser.
But the biggest improvement or the biggest addition that the Geo will have is a giant backpack.
It's like one of the regular cargo boxes, you can just pop it in and it'll fill it with oil as you mine.
And it's got a little multi-tool storage on the bottom where you have your multi-tool mining gadget and the big FPS tractor beam.
You can also bring spare containers, so once the container on your bag is full you can then detach it and replace it with a new one.
But the most unique thing about the Geo is a new functionality, jump and hover.
So the jumping is my favourite bit of it, it lets you jump quite high, you've got to charge up the jump first of course,
but then you can leap quite big distances.
You can enforce the jump or simmer down the jump or the landing process by firing the thrusters.
You can press space to jump and then press, keep pressing space or hold it to give a thrust and kind of fly.
While you're in the air you can maintain a small hover, you can adjust your aiming as your landing.
If you get stuck in a like a ravine or something you can jump out to escape. It's hilarious, it's fun.
We also did some updates to the existing Atlas, so it has now a health bar integrated into the frame, so you always see the health setters of your Atlas.
It also has a battery slot now, not used as of now, but will be used once the engineering gameplay comes in.
And apart from that we did some tweaks to the animations, so there are some death animations that we now have.
We've added some small thrusters that allow you to land a little bit more gracefully when you're falling from a cliff or when you jump out of a ship or falling from a greater height.
I'm a vehicle artist but I love big robots just as much.
It's much smaller than the rock, so you can compact it back in the cargo bay of a bigger ship, much easier.
I personally enjoy it when I visit some big stompy robots.
So we hope that you are excited for the new Atlas Geo. We are really happy to give it out the way it is right now.
It gives us also some opportunity to revisit some of the FPS mining and IOC mining.
And we are happy to continue developing or continue improving or expanding on the Atlas going forward.

segments.text: Engineering. The next major step forward in multi-crew gameplay. Built on top of the
in-development resource networking system. It's self a harbinger, a fire, and a new
reality for all life aboard spacecraft. It's been the subject of CitizenCon presentations,
Q&As on Star Citizen Live, explorations on inside Star Citizen, and frequent discussion
by many of the content creators in our community. And on this final episode of ISC Before Hiatus
and we turn all of our attentions towards CitizenCon, we invited Torsten, Bastion, and Guillermo to
update us once again on the current intention and implementation of engineering. And what you
can expect when the first iteration makes its way into the persistent universe.
Resource Network enables us to actually give you the gameplay that you were always looking for,
which is having meaningful multi-crew gameplay, which means that it really makes sense to have
multiple people running around on your ship, and that wouldn't be possible without the
Resource Network. So we say the Resource Network is a system that allows all the items and components
that are part of the ship to talk to each other. Every ground vehicle, every base, everything that
runs in Star Citizen with resources. Fundamentally, Resource Network is a
replacement for the pipe system we had in the past that you might have heard about.
We chose a similar system, basically doing most of what we're doing right now with the
Resource Network, but in a way that was not as scalable as what we intend to do.
So right now we just have one type of hydrogen fuel, but if we want to extend that in the future to
having multiple types that have some specific benefits on the thrusters, it's very easy now
to add that resource. It's just a data setup. So Resource Network is the underlying technology
for the system to work, and engineering is the gameplay we intend to have on top of this technology
so that players may experience it. Your ship flies because you know the thrusters get fueled,
the power plants output power that the weapons and the sails and also the thrusters use.
Engineering is all about both maximizing the use you get out of the Resource Network,
and also getting the Resource Network itself going so that you're not dead in the water.
It's all things that players will be able to interact with. They will have to dedicate
roles in their ships so that crew members are assigned to fixing those issues,
and they can encounter more dynamic situations that will not happen in the systems.
The goal right now is to have all the components on the ship being physicalized. That means that
things that will take damage will be the components. That then means that those components
are the reasons to the failure of your ship. We have the power plants which generate the
energy that your ship consumes. You have the ship generators which take in some of that energy to
convert it to shield power. You have a radar system that allows you to target the signatures
of ships around you. You have crewers that generate the crew and resource.
It is all the weapons that you have. It's the Quantum Drive, but there are also new components
that will be added to the mix, and that is the relay with its fuses. Then there's the life support
generator. The biggest thing we are aiming for is switching from your health pool of the bespoke
ship to just moving that completely over to the physicalized component. So damaging the component
is damaging your ship. I think this is the part where the biggest change for the players
happen because there the gameplay of repair comes in, and then you can revitalize your ship.
So you can actually use your formerly dead-in-the-water ship after exchanging or repairing the components.
We mentioned one of the new components which is the life support generator. So let's talk about
life support. The life support. Does all the tasks necessary to maintain the life support inside the
ship? So it's the temperature, it's the atmosphere composition, it's the pressure inside the room.
Your main responsibility is making sure that there is always enough life support resource
produced to maintain a healthy atmosphere in the ship. So making sure that all the CO2 that you
breathe out is actually converted into O2 again, or if you vented a room that the room is filled
again, if your room is getting too hot it's cooled down again. So it's all about managing this resource
inside the rooms. And as already mentioned in the previous episodes,
it's life support management is also a good way to counter fire.
Another aspect the players have to counter or react to is misfires on components.
Misfires are something that is already in the game in some form. Thrust or surges,
city generator failure, stuff like that. Or you have to expand the need a bit. And pretty much
the idea is that items that are damaged, that are too hot, or that for example are very old and
degraded will start misfiring. In some cases that will be that it will take some extra damage.
In other cases it will stop working for a while. Other times it will work indefinitely until an
engineer comes by and manages to do some repairs. And some of the worst cases would be starting a
fire or in the case of for example power plants, engaging in a critical reactor failure and taking
the ship with them. There was a chance that if the power plant reaches zero health it will run
into a critical failure and that critical failure then will cause the entire ship to explode.
It will give the player the time frame to react to that. So either by removing the component and
throwing it out of the door and preventing your ship to explode or even countering it by repairing
the component and bringing it up to life again. For the initial release we have a limited amount
of misfires but we are preparing the system or we did prepare the system to scale well
for the future so we can introduce multiple misfires and that leads us to damage penetration.
So damage penetration is a simplified version of what we'll be getting eventually with a more
physicalized system but essentially what it means is that now certain types of weapons can
penetrate through the hull of the ship. This is a function of the weapon itself, its penetration
values and also the armor of the ship which can be depleted over time. So if you use ballistic
you have a higher penetration which allows you to cut through the armor more deeply and touch
the components inside the ship directly. As opposed to this you can also have energy weapons which
will be more effective at melting down the armor. The goal here is that you first need to bring down
the armor health value to get to the fullest potential of your penetrating weapons then you
can penetrate the ship and actually damage the components that sit inside the ship and not on
the outside of the hull. Obviously there's degrees to this, large and ballistic weapons may have
enough penetration against smaller ships that it would be able to penetrate directly but it's
you know it's all of a game of choices and it's gonna depend on your ships and your weapons.
So with damage penetration and misfires happening that brings us to repair.
As your fight progresses and components take damage in your ship it becomes a duty of some of your
crew members to first investigate what are the issues caused by the damage and go there to
physically replace the parts in your ship. So you have your multi-tools so you have the
savage and repair and the repair part of it also affects now ship components precisely like what
you see in the arena command. You will be able to repair items that were fully destroyed.
You will not be able to repair the item to its fullest so you cannot repair an item that got
fully destroyed to 100 health again so to repair your ship components to the fullest
you actually have to bring them to the shop again and do the station repair.
Or if you did think ahead and brought spare items with you you can simply exchange them to
pristine new ones but with the caveat it only works just as a reminder for size one and size
two components size three and above cannot be exchanged using the tractor beam detach and attach
so now that we looked at what your responsibilities are in the physical space running around in
your ship let's take a look at what you do on the virtual part which is power management and
analysis of your ship on the engineering screen. So the first thing that you will see is the 3D
view of your ship that highlights the location of all the ship components and how they are actually
connected where the relay positions are what the status of the relays are you will see the
holograms of each component. As you can see they have different colors what they are representing
is the overall state of the item so an item that is very damaged or is on fire or is not getting
enough power will be in a critical state. Items that are less damaged are receiving only partial
resources or are going through a misfire may have moderate colors and items that are otherwise fine
will have to function on our blue cords. The biggest change that happened to the engineering
UI screen is basically the power management part of it. We moved away completely from slider control
for every individual item. There is indicator now for fuel this is not relevant for the initial
release but it will be relevant for the future. Next to it you'll see the power plant the power plant
segments gives you an idea of how many power segments you can distribute to the ship items.
And on the right of each of the power bars you can generally see the temperature bar.
If it goes into overheating the item will stop both consuming or producing and it will be completely
inoperable until it cools down again so that means that assigning power to your coolers in advance is
probably a good idea if you're going into a fight. All the items on your ship generate heat so this
is where you can see the amount of heat that each item has accumulated and you can see the amount of
coolant that you are producing and whether or not you are also running deficit. So what you want to do
is put as much power as you can into the coolers until your items do not overheat but do not assign
more resources than necessary because you are running a limited pool of resources. The same applies

that the demand is fulfilled in your ship. If your demand isn't fulfilled it will cause some failures.

warning you will be able to see it as a notification. Take a look at it go to the item or just remove it.
So you have an option that allows you to basically log the controls so that you or the pilot which has

controls so by locking this you are able to override the MFD settings to only have it
being authoritative from the engineering station. You are able to take the power assignment you have
under given time and save it locally on your computer meaning that when you fly again with this

segments.text: There are lots of ways to bring life to the worlds of Star Citizen.
Whether that's the people that inhabit them, the structures they build,
or the coffee cups and food wrapper decor scattered across their desk.
But perhaps nothing quite as much as nature's inhabitants.
Now animals, creatures, fauna, whatever you call them,
have been one of the long, unfulfilled promises of the persistent universe
since planets were first introduced in Alpha 3.0.

with the first of a new herd of offerings that will continue on subsequent releases.

and get just a small glimpse into what went into their creation.

They bring a sense of life to a world,
gives an environment a sense of that it's a lived in space.
There's a lot going on on the planets, but it can feel at times like
there's not a huge amount going on.
But with the introduction of creatures, that all changes.
We have now the ability to create life wherever you look.
It just takes the game to another level of breathtaking.
It adds believability to the experience that
I don't think any feature so far has come to the level of adding immersion that Fauna has.
In Alpha 3.23, we're adding two new creatures.
One is the Maric and one is the Copian.
When you're kind of exploring these planets,
we are introducing a whole range of different creatures going forward into the future.
Well, you want to start off simple, right?
You look at it, you're like, oh cool, you know, should we work on these big creatures straight away?
Or should we ground down, make sure the pipeline works, make sure the basics work?
What's more simple than a dog cat and a bird?

and you see a bunch of birds and life on the surfaces where you wouldn't before.

title: Star Citizen | Behind the Ships: MISC Fortune

segments.text: The MISX Fortune is a solo player salvage vessel.
It's similar to the Vulture in size and utility.
It is technically a variant of the previous ship, the prospector,
but obviously there's many, many differences you can benefit from.
What we've done is we've sort of tried to push the automatic cargo dispensing mechanism
that's on the Vulture a little bit further
and sort of we've combined some of MISX exterior cargo hold type of mechanic
with the salvaging mechanism.
What we're doing with the salvage on the Fortune is we're having the cargo that gets created as you salvage
be stored on the exterior as well.
When you go back to the salvage station, there's a panel and you can hit auto eject
or you can just eject it manually and every time you eject,
it will eject it out onto the exterior of the ship and it will automatically snap it to their cargo grid.
It is pretty cool that you can eject the crate simultaneously on each side of the ship
if you want to seeing them two salvage stations working together in tandem is kind of a new thing for us,
so pretty neat.
The ship really makes use of all the available space inside of it.
We did complete component pass so it has everything exposed
and it has a similar interior as the prospector so it's got the same hab and the bathroom and all that
but we've extended it out so that you can walk from the front all the way to the back.
And then we've got an elevator in the rear for you to be able to bring those boxes in and out if you want to
or additional items so just imagine you're going out into space to salvage some wrecks.
You strip the metal off the surface of the vehicle, it'll create boxes on the side of the ship
and then in addition to that you want to pull off some of the weapons.
If they're small enough you can actually put them in the elevator in the rear as storage.
So it's not a dedicated cargo area on the inside but it should be big enough for you to grab some of the smaller components
if you're able to salvage those.
It's got this double cockpit that allows you to see just outside anywhere in any direction.
It's very similar to the prospector so if you like the prospector cockpit you can allow the fortune cockpit.
We're also going to be going out with the new dashboard that's been created by the UI team from MISC.
That'll be on the fortune and the prospector going forward.
Like anything else between ships in Star Citizen it's a trade-off.
Well both the fortune and vulture are single-seat salvage ships.
The fortune is going to focus a little bit more on convenience for the user because it has one salvage head
versus the vultures too. It's not going to salvage quite as efficiently.
So you might be able to salvage and do hull scraping a little bit faster still using the vulture.
The advantage is that it might be just a little bit easier to operate.
You won't have to be rearranging things as much as you would with the vulture.
And having two systems in play makes it maybe a little bit easier for the user to keep salvaging.
I think that the team did a really good job. Shout out to Chris Smith, Jen, Joë, also Chad's team, and Pierre-Lude and Mitch.
They did a great job on the new tech.

segments.text: So the RSI Aurora is the quintessential starter star citizenship.
For the people that have been with the project a long time, it was one of the first ships that they saw it.
So it gave you that first experience of boarding your own ship, exploring the interior, although limited,
and then finally climbing into the pilot seat and then taking off for your first mission or exploration.
Whilst the game has evolved over the last decade and we have learnt a lot more about building spaceships in that time,
we felt that now was the right time to go revisit the Aurora series.
Doing a follow-up of the original Aurora is actually quite the task because you have to make sure that it's as beloved as the original.
The Mk2 combines the classic DNA of the original Mk1 Aurora and then brings it up to modern day standards,
both in terms of visuals and gameplay.
RSI tend to want to kind of push the boundaries a little bit.
They want to look back and see what they've done in the past and what was successful.
But they're not scared to really embrace new ideas.
We've tried to keep the overall proportions and styling of the base of Aurora with the Mk2, but we just tried to sharpen it up.
It has a really angular style. It looks really sleek.
Everything flows and it has this sort of layered, armoured look.
The circular door is still there to enter the ship, but it's hidden by the newer layered RSI door designs.
We still have these really iconic four wings down the sides that give the ship its length.
There's also some doors that open up and show the V-talls underneath, which are these fans that help support the ship while it's changing trajectories.
There's even a cool new feature where you can vault onto the top of the ship over the front canopy.
My favourite part of that entire ship is actually the back section.
It has tons of detail that all lines up towards the centre of the ship.
Something we were keen to follow up with is some of the RSI ships have transforming states, such as the Scorpius.
We were playing with the idea of, like, do we open the wings? Do we not open the wings?
And as soon as we kind of started playing with the idea and seeing how it looked, it just felt natural.
The base of Aurora Mk2 comes with four size two weapon hardpoints, as well as four size two missile hardpoints, each defaulting to two size one missiles.
The guns are actually attached to what the wings are attached to, so when the wings pop off, the guns are still attached to the ship.
So if you lose your wings, you're not totally out of the fight?
No, so if you lose your wings, you'll lose your missiles and you'll lose the VTAL if you lose the bottom wings.
When we were doing the original design for the Mk2 Aurora, one thing that came up was, do we want to do variants or do modules?
In terms of production, the variant of a ship is actually a lot of work on our part.
You have to redo modelling, you have to almost rethink the whole entire ship.
The ship now, instead of being a variant, comes with two different modules.
And the advantage of modules is you buy one Aurora Mk2 and forever in the future, when upgrades happen to the ship, you can grab that module and then add it to your own ship.
The TS module, or what we internally refer to as the cargo module, provides an additional six SEU cargo on a drop lift, which takes the whole cargo capacity of the Aurora Mk2 with it equipped.
The TS module is a pretty competitive type of ship.
One of the big changes with the TS module and the base Aurora is the cargo is held intimately rather than underslung underneath, so it's more protected.
So it's great for somebody who's just getting started, who wants to do hauling missions before upgrading to something bigger like a Zeus.
Or you can either go with the Defence module, which adds eight S2 missiles and also one S1 shield generator in the back of it.
So if you add eight S2 missiles, you're much more lethal. And if you add another S1 shield, you're adding 50% more shield to your ship.

segments.text: Earlier this year in Victus we introduced the Greycat MTC which was the first in the family of
ground vehicles from Greycat. The MTC was designed as this sort of utilitarian all-purpose
rover style vehicle that allows two players to just bomb around the battlefield exploring,
storage on board for whatever they need and then as well having mission storage boxes on the back.
So really there's a ground vehicle capable of doing the majority of our ground vehicle
and today we're introducing the MTC which is your mobile defense center.
The MTC is the ultimate ground support vehicle that you can take into battle.
It's designed to give you that little bit extra protection.
There's no vehicle that's better to support your team.
The first thing you're going to notice when you see the MTC is the PDT on the back
and point defense turret. The PDT itself is new, it's a ballistic gattling version of the existing
bearing point defense turret we have elsewhere in the game. Obviously being a ballistic it has
finite ammo so this will need to go back to a location to reload but the trade-off for that
is that it has an increased alpha damage so it is more useful against shielded and armored targets.
So the reason we decided to put a PDT on the ground vehicle was because when you have events like
Jumptown and people are there lauding their ships and getting other bits and pieces,
you're very vulnerable to attack. They're giving them a different means to actually defend themselves
or if they're under on. The PDT on the MDC is swappable so that means you can have the missile
variants, the gattling variants and the laser variants. The missile and the laser variants
is now available in 4.4 within in-game stores. Driving the MDC around is very much like driving
the MDC around, its handling is almost identical. It's capable of getting to places the MDC is,
capable of getting and can be carried in the same sort of vehicles as the MDC.
But whilst you're driving around the PDT is automatically engaging threats against you as a player
whether that's incoming ordnance or ships. But as an added bonus it is also very useful as a base
defence mechanism. You can park this vehicle up, leave it there and then it will continue the same
role of defending against targeted ordnance and ships whilst you're outside the vehicle.
The XU is a mix between utilitarian and minimalistic. We wanted to find good balance between those.
The MXC is a really nice chassis to work with. We thought about the different variants when we
were designing the base chassis and I think it lends itself really well. It kind of leans into
that military idea of they don't want to be making everything from scratch. They want parts to be
serviceable, they want to be interchangeable. We've tried to keep the overall silhouette of the
vehicle and its overall size as close to the main chassis as we can but then when it jumps into action

a little bit greater visibility not only of the sky but also of the surrounding area.
You can see the engineering that's gone into it and I think it's really successful in conveying
what its purpose is. The interior is based on the teenage engineering design rounded corner

title: Star Citizen | Behind the Ships: Kruger L-21 Wolf

segments.text: I would describe Kruger as beautiful, bald and elegant, not afraid to make a statement.
Unlike Origin, Kruger ships have a certain retro feel to them but still feel upmarket.
The L21 is a life fighter designed to be fast, agile and nimble.
The trade-off is that you have to take extra care when getting into battle
and you can't take the hits, you have to avoid them.
When I first saw the concept I thought this is really amazing and I can't wait to walk on it.
It looks also very challenging because of the sloping shapes on the difficult surfaces.
Instead of kind of having layered surfaces like a lot of other star citizen ships have,
the surfaces are very clean, very smooth.
The direction for the ship was to make it sleek, aerodynamic and aggressive.
The exterior of the ship has the silhouette of a spit fighter but it looks a lot more
resting modern and futuristic.
We definitely looked at a lot of level 2 aircraft and that's kind of where the influence came from.
The tail is shorter so it has this very aggressive nose pointing upward stance when it's landed.
It kind of feels like an animal waiting to bounce.
That's why she's called the wolf.
The engine assaults on the wings I think create a very nice silhouette especially from the top.
I'm also very very happy with the form language that we managed to do on it.
We decided to expose a lot of greebling, we decided to expose a lot of the engine itself.
It primarily pipes, the heat travels down it and it really promotes how strong that the ship
actually is. It highlights the grace of the ship.
The vehicle has two sizeful gaitlins that can gimbal five degrees in all directions.
You have four missiles in the left wing and you have four missiles in the right wing.
I'm very happy with the deploy animation of the weapons.
That's something that really any other ship does to this extent
when we have the weapons completely hidden in the fuselage which creates a very very smooth package.
The cockpit's a really comfy place to be as you'll see when you look out from the ship
your great visibility from the left the right and the head of you.
I just love the cockpit it just looks so slick.
The dash is such a strong shape I've not seen the shape before in any of the other ships.
You'll notice in between your legs a brand new clock which I believe is the first that
you've implemented in a vehicle.
Yeah, you had to do the clock.
Yeah, the clock looks great. It looks like a swiss timepiece that's in between your legs
just so you can keep track of servo time.
You have to stop saying in between your legs.
What do you think? The thing was an idea I kind of had when I noticed from certain angles especially
the nose kind of had some shapes reminiscent of a boat so I was kind of thinking might be
interesting to add something like a keel also just to make the silhouette a bit more interesting
especially when I'm diving inside.
And there's also once again something that I don't really think any other ship at this point
and it just adds to there being a transition from landed mode to flight mode.
This vehicle is for somebody who wants a nice sleek elegant design.
People who are into sports cars I hope they will appreciate the surfacing on the ship.
I hope people who like a retro sci-fi will appreciate the big engine that sells on the wingtips.
I hope everyone likes it.
It's very unique the scornet and the water ship that looks like it.

and I think you should fly it.
