title: Inside Star Citizen: Alpha 3.24.2 - Zeus and MFDs

segments.text: First introduced at last year's CitizenCon, the RSI Zeus is steadily working its way through the ship pipeline to its intended release.
And on this week's show, we'll take a look at two of its variants, as well as the new MFD rework that you've seen glimpses of here and there.
It's a multifunctional show. Let's get to it.
The RSI Zeus Mk.2 is a reimagining of the original RSI Zeus.
The Zeus was the first mass-made human exploration ship that was capable of doing quantum travel.
We didn't want to just make the Zeus again. We wanted to pay homage to what made the Zeus important.
What made it iconic back then? We wanted to give that an update and bring it up to modern-day visuals and make sure it really feels RSI.
It's RSI style, but we feel it's almost an improvement upon the style. It's sort of an evolution of the style.
And so players will appreciate the consistency with other RSI ships, but you can see the technological advancement of RSI.
You may remember the Zeus from our episode in Jump Points a few weeks ago on Insight Star Citizen.
It was very good.
It was very good, Jared tells me.
The Zeus is a great stepping stone ship. So you've got your starter ship originally.
You've dipped your toes in a few gameplay loops and you just want to be able to do a bit more.
The Zeus has allowed you to do that with some friends.
So yeah, it supports up to three crew members, but you can fly it yourself if you want.
And if you've got a buddy, they can man the turrets.
The Zeus is for me probably some of the best looking ships we've ever produced for Star Citizen.
I think they really set a new visual standard in both their shape and style.
So when we release the Zeus, it comes with both the ES and the CL, both together in the same patch.
The ES is the exploration focused variant of the Zeus.
So it has a modest size cargo bay, larger hydrogen and quantum fuel tanks,
a larger radar and a more spacious living area.
The CL, the cargo version, maximizes its cargo capacity.
It does that by shunting the sort of central bulkhead towards the front of the ship.
So that increases the cargo capacity from 32 to 128 SEU at the expense of just really cramming in the living quarters to be much more compact.
The exterior of the Zeus ES has got that very kind of iconic RSI hour head shape.
We tried to stick to what was like the homage that the concept made of the first Zeus.
It keeps the kind of central fuselage.
You've got this big kind of central mass with these lovely kind of quite fast and aggressive looking wings.
And they kind of just help to make it feel quite aggressive and quite sharp,
which I think builds on what RSI is a brand, kind of really about.
The big details on the flat surfaces, the mix of materials, I think is very well balanced.
I'm still a massive fan of the underside.
Undersides of our ship sometimes get a little bit under looked or overlooked.
Sorry.
Yeah, but I think the underside, the belly, originally the plan was for it to be kind of completely smooth and completely all one surface.
But as we started to work it up, the artist that were working on it kind of like,
can we add a little bit of recesses, can we add a little bit of relief into this shape just to kind of help build on the believability?
I think it was a real success.
So weaponry wise, across all of them, the pilot has access to twin size four guns.
And the side seats have access to the remote turrets.
When we look at the difference between the ES and the cargo, with the cargo,
we want to add a little bit more structure and believability into the exterior of the ship.
This is supposed to carry a lot more weight.
So we want to kind of bulk up the main structural points.
So we've got some large additional bracing down the center.
And then the other thing that a cargo version is going to require is some additional thrust.
So we want to kind of bulk up the main thrusters at the rear that allowed kind of take off.
And those kind of downward pointing thrusters of crone size and add to that believability that,
you know, this vehicle can lift a bit more weight than the base version.
So if we start at the front of the ship, it's quite a tight space.
One of the things that we kind of really realized early on with the vehicle is that
we crammed a lot of stuff into the space that we had to play with.
So the cockpit is quite tight.
You've got a nice kind of three person cockpit up the front.
And the seating arrangement echoes that kind of arrow shape that we see on the exterior of the ship.
And that just helps to make the pilot have the important up front seat,
but also just ties everything together a little bit, which is lovely.
As we go back through the ship, we go into the airlock and the engineering area.
This area changed quite a bit during the vehicle's development.
We actually opened this space up a little bit.
We took out one of the bulkheads.
One of the things we realized as we kind of got into production was that there was maybe a few too many doors.
It really was the ideal place to kind of remove one of those and open that area up a little bit.
So we've got this engineering section that has the kind of main docking collar.
And it also has the ladder exit.
So we've got our kind of two front exits on the vehicle.
And then as we go back through the corridor section, we hear we have like a bit of a crossroads.
So you can either go into the kitchen area, which still has its nice window and looks out and it's beautiful and perfect.
Or on the right we've got the habitation area, where we've got three beds, toilet, a nice little seating area, lockers,
and everything you need really in terms of a hub.
And then as we go into the back of the ship, that's really where we get to our larger ship components and our cargo area.
With the cargo version, the clipper, there's obviously a lot more space dedicated to cargo compared to the base version.
To achieve that, what we've had to do is adjust some of the kind of like the rear layout of the ships.
We had to rearrange the components so that they're closer up to the doorway.
And we had to move the weapon locker from the corridor into the actual cargo hold.
So there was a lot of rearranging.
But what that does by us is enough space to fit the kind of extra cargo in.
We've also had to sacrifice some of the kitchen area in the habitation.
You lose the sofa and the nice seating area.
But on the positive, we get much more cargo space, which for a dedicated cargo ship is the most important thing.
You'll notice that on the floor, there'll be blue trimming exactly where the player can place cargo.
It'll be a lot easier for the player to know where you can access the components versus where you can place cargo on the sides.
This has been a great first full ship from Concept to Release for the Montreal vehicle team.
This is one ship that took an entire year to build.
Like the amount of work that goes into these ships is insane, both in art and design.
They built on kind of what they'd learned with the cutters and really just done a fantastic job in taking what was, you know, the original vision of the ship
and really delivering it in something that I think it looks great, it should play great.
And I think they just did a fantastic job across the board.
To me, you know, the final product shows there's nothing in any other game that can come close to level detail.
The amount of thought that got put into every component bay, everything, you know, is in its place.
So the Zeus is another great addition to the fleet of ships and star citizen and being our site obviously has that special touch,
sharing the name of our company and founder.
And we are excited to see this ship set foot in the verse and push along the RSI style ahead of a big year for RSI ships.
Ships done set foot, John, they fly.
Got a little bit.
Just being argumentative.
MFDs and the ship HUD in the PU, it's old and the actual UI itself is very small.
One color, they're all in one color.
Text is too small to read.
It's very samey, right?
It has a bunch of stuff on it that you don't really use.
Not very user, new user friendly.
Any user friendly?
Yeah.
Any user friendly.
It was good for its time.
It did the job.
It got us where we are today.
But it's time for something new and that's what we're going to talk about.
The reason why we're doing this now is because we had a lot of time during the development of Squadron to create an expandable
and a more robust system for MFDs.
We have a bunch of super nice MFDs ready for Squadron and now we're moving them over to Star Citizen.
It's also really good to bring it over now because we've got the new resource network system.
So we need to have the MFDs here to support that new gameplay.
Initial release, there'll be five visual styles to the MFDs and the HUDs.
There's Aegis.
It's very militaristic and it's very sleek.
Anvil is great.
I love the green colour of Anvil.
It feels a lot more like an F-16 cockpit.
Drake is my favourite.
It's retro and Blade Runner and CRTs.
There's Argo.
It really feels like a piece of industrial equipment which is what the brand is going for.
And there's the generic style that will support all the other ship manufacturers for the time being.
For this release, the MFDs are getting nine different views.
Oh, how many is that even?
Well, let's go through it.
Well, that was Self-Status.
Self-Status includes all of the critical information about your ship,
dependent on your current operator mode.
So you'll have your ammo numbers in guns mode.
You'll have your missile arming in missile mode.
And your fuel readouts in quantum mode.
There's also a unique version for turrets as well.
We have taken away a lot of, well, faff from there.
So this is simpler than before.
It's more condensed and it links into the new systems that have been developed in terms of vehicle features.
For example, it shows your updated gimbal modes.
And it also shows your current weapon group, which is a new thing as well.
Target status is the same thing, but it gives you the information about the target that you have currently selected.
It's mostly going to be for a lot of players.
This ship, Paulo, you're going to want to see, am I dealing some damage or not?
You will also have the emissions, so you know what missile to use against them.
And you will see their names so you know that you're not shooting the wrong person.
It's not as much information because obviously if you want to see how much ammo they've got, you've got to scan them.
But it will show you their health, it will show you their faction, it will show you their velocity.
Weapon config is entirely new. It links into the new weapon grouping system.
So it will list out every single weapon on your ship.
The ammo that you have, they'll light up if they're selected.
And also it allows you to assign them to one of four custom groups.
So you can have any combination of weapons that you want firing at the same time.
And it makes it easy to see which group of weapons you're firing.
And if you just don't assign one of those groups, if you feel like, well, four's too many, I just use two anyway.
Well, you can just assign to two of them and you'll be fine.
This will be valuable so the player can in combat switch between different modes depending on kind of distance and what kind of weapons they want to use.
On a day to day, you might be tracking down a particular target.
It is a subject of a mission and you know that a certain weapon is going to be more effective against them than another,
or a certain weapon combination is going to be more effective.
You can stick them all in one group and have quick access to that.
Shields is pretty much the same as what it was.
You can control each of your shield faces if you have four shield faces.
If you have one, you can control the whole thing.
And it gives you a reset button so you can set it all back to default.
And also you can see your total shield usage out of the maximum.
For the time being, this is going to be the same thing that you're already used to.
And along with that are scanning and communications.
Scanning's been moved from the HUD to an MFD state.
The new screens, the biggest one is power management.
It's a simplified version of what you'll find on an engineering terminal,
but it's for daily use for the pilot.
It's using the full power of the resource network system.
And it gives it to you right there in the pilot's seat.
So you can do the full assignments as you like them if you're flying solo.
This is also where you will see your emissions.
So if you're doing anything stealthy, you go into power management.
You set your settings to low and you will see your emissions adjust accordingly.
You can turn on and off different systems in the ship.
You can apply different levels of power to each system.
You can see your total output, how much you're using,
and you can also see different status readouts for those systems.
So if something has run out of power or it's offline,
it'll also represent that on the power management MFD.
Along with that is the diagnostics view.
The diagnostics view is where you go to check in on your ship.
If something's not feeling right, well, maybe check diagnostics.
It will show you the where that component is taken,
as well as its current health and its status, whether it has any errors.
And there'll be a summary at the top of the screen
that shows you how many of your components have errors.
And last, what I'm really excited about is the configuration screen.
It takes a lot of these settings that were hidden away in the options menu
or just in the back end and puts them right there for you to toggle in world on your MFD screen.
The configuration view is great.
You can now turn off unwanted UI if you really wish to.
You can turn off the cast, which is my favourite part.
If you have screens on the top left and top right of your screen,
then you can turn off those casts now to clear the UI a little bit.
So this configuration screen allows you to configure a few aspects
of some different MFD states, as well as what goes on your HUD and how that looks.
You can finally control what goes on your HUD.
We can finally control what goes on our HUD.
Yeah.
So let's talk about the HUD.
Using the configuration screen, you can choose whether or not you're showing your MFD casts,
which are simplified and more tactile versions of the self-states and target status screen.
Functionality-wise, it's stuff you know already.
You have your velocity, you have your afterburner, you have your amunciators,
and you have different indicators.
They show critical information when you can't look at your dashboard in front of you,
so if you're in a fighter and you're looking up in the sky,
you can still see that, as well as allowing you to still see that information
when you're in precision targeting mode.
We've decided to clear up all of the nonsense we have in the middle
and kind of make it out of the way if you're in the middle of the screen, so...
What took so long, Joe?
I'm sorry. It wasn't good.
Oh, God.
We've also done a little bit of work making the radar and the HUD feel more diegetic
and making it look like it actually exists in the cockpit
with grounding effects and emission rate origin points, as well.
It all just feels so much better. It feels real.
So with this new ship and vehicle HUD, it's just going to be a clearer experience overall.
It's going to be clearer in the sense that you don't have stuff in your face all the time.
It's going to be clearer in the sense that you can actually read the UI,
so I think you'll be very happy with it.
It's going to be such a nice thing to just be out in space and be able to see space, right?
So what did we learn this week?
Well, we learned that the Zeus is the first ship made by the newly established Montreal vehicle team.
That the MFD rework is an exciting and easily usable and customizable upgrade to what we've had before.
And that it plugs nicely into the upcoming resource network and engineering work scheduled for Alpha 4.0,
which we'll, of course, we'll be showcasing next week.
For Inside Star Citizen, I'm Jared Huckabee.
Thanks for letting us share the people and process of game development with you,
and we'll see you all here next week.

title: Inside Star Citizen | Dev Diary: Digital Hairdresser

segments.text: This was unintended. That's the first thing I must say.
My career took a curve. I was a lead character artist at another company.
One of the things that scared me the most at that time was hair, because it is one of the hardest tasks.
And I just tackled it so well, I guess, that I started to get praise for it.
Praise in a way that I never got as a character artist.
And that's how I went. I never planned to be a digital hairdresser of any sort.
I've been in love with Star Citizen since ever.
It's been actually my dream for all along. When I started learning character art, this is what I wanted to work.
When I started here, one of the things people were making fun of me, former colleagues, were like,
oh great, Andre, you just signed a contract to make hair for a game. Everyone wears a helmet.
And that made me think.
Rest assured, nowadays I'm proud to log in to Star Citizen and just see that a lot of people is now wearing their hairs and not the helmets.
When I got here, the first thing was to try not to scrap everything that was made.
Obviously, there was a lot of things that were properly made.
They just wouldn't fit for every purpose that we wanted.
The first hair I created took me a bit of time. The first results were kind of disappointing.
I was still learning the tools, learning the process, learning the new engine that we use.
But after like three weeks, I managed to create one hair. We finally took it to a meeting.
My first time in front of CR, I actually made sure I read everything that CR has written about hair that was on our register.
So I knew what he wanted. I think that was kind of smart because it had an impact on him immediately.
The next morning after that meeting, I'll wake up with a message on our creative chat saying something.
How happy it was that we had finally someone that was tackling hair in the way that he wanted.
I'm like, all right, we're on the right path, I thought.
Doing this process, Ian actually told me,
Okay, Andre, what do you need to make this work for both Squadron 42 and Star Citizen?
And I'm like, he wanted to have 70 hairs from February till December,
so that we can do the first chapters of Squadron 42.
Doing my maths really fast, if I was to do it myself, it would take like two years.
Even if I take like three to five days per hair, normally a hair before I arrived was taking 20 to 40 days.
The only solution was to hire more hands, hire more people, and I needed people that would
hit the ground running. It had to be people that I knew that could do the work.
And in that sense, I presented the proposal to Ian and to CR.
They agreed to everything and that's how we did it. We basically put the guys in.
Instead of 70 hairs, by December we had 130 hairs because we did not only do the Squadron ones,
we actually revamped the character customizer. We added beers, which weren't even in the plan
back then. It was a bad, risky bet, but I took the process under my wing. I grabbed the guys
and it worked. And for that, I got some praise and got some recognition in the company, which
comes with the risk that I have taken, of course.
So where do we start with the hair? There must be an idea first, an intention, of course.
Star Citizen is a bit different from Squadron. In Squadron we're trying to do digital clones.
Obviously, in that case, we're going to take as much pictures, as much references of the real person,
and try to mimic that into the video game. As for Star Citizen, which is a bit more broad,
we sometimes require a concept. Sometimes we have a more broader idea that we want to go.
We are production artists. We are not concept artists, so that's not what we do.
What we really need to work is that the idea comes solid at us and it's very clear what's intended.
Whatever references we can use, we'll make a mood board and from there, start our own development.
It's important to understand that the system that I implemented here, it kind of removes
from the artist the ability to mess it up in the sense that I control the textures and the shaders,
so that means the beginning of the process and the ending of the process. I've tested them,
I make sure they work, and so I give to the artist the pleasurable part of just doing the asset
itself, and therefore there's no fruit salad. What we want is basically a quality that is standard,
that stays the same throughout the game, and if I gave them the ability to create their own textures,
we would have hairs, some would be very thick, some would be very thin, some would be different,
and it would render different. So I remove these two parts of the process of the equation by sorting
it myself, giving them the only the pleasurable part, that I don't have any other word for it.
He's not wrong.
Enjoyable, enjoyable, enjoyable. I guess.
Making hair for games has a lot of limitations to it. Our game being fast-paced and all MMO,
the way to keep it performing and the way to keep it working is by trying to establish limits
of how far you can go. When I started, I remember the lead tech artist telling me,
Andre, there's no limit to what you can do, just go, there's no budget of try count,
there's no budget, and I'm like, how can that be? I mean, I've been doing games for a while,
and there is limitations, okay? He was just letting me be free enough to create,
and letting me establish the limits so that they can then adapt. I was very conservative,
we all have performant hairs. Some in Squadron 42 are a bit heavier because we just need to
hit that quality bar, but mostly are all very performant. What you do is just use what you
need and you don't use what you don't need, basically. What are you working on for 2025?
2025 comes with creatures and more hairs for the character customizing. That's the main thing.
There's also armors that are going to start to have a bit of hair. Hair, not hair, human hair,
but types of fur or types of synthetic hair. We created a lot of hairs which are recognizable.
We were trying to break barriers. The character customizer is like this nowadays,
because we were trying to push the shader and see where we could go. Tools programmers and shader
programmers were coming to me and saying, hey, Andre, I didn't know our shader could do this type
of things. As I got this type of feedback, I was, okay, let's push this and see how far we can go.
So we have a bit of a range which is a bit too wide for now in terms of hairs that we're using.
One of the last meetings with CR regarding this aspect, he just told me, Andre, what we need now
is Jared's hair, is Andre's hair. Move away from the outrages, move away from the military
hair styles. That's the direction for now to get established a good solid base of hairs. On the
creatures, we're going a bit wilder now. We're starting to push the limits as the fully covered
with fur creatures and stuff like that. Before, we started with small patches of fur here and
there on the creatures and now we're just making all things together. Well, I'm eager to do hair
styles that will be longer than the limitation that we currently have. Our current limitation is
the shoulders simply because of the way the armors work and the helmets work, and we don't want it
to be clipping all along. So I'm really looking at the day that we can make hairs that are longer,
and I'd love to do like a big dreadlock that goes straight down.
Yeah, so I'm really, really proud of my team. Everything that I said here is basically a
teamwork. My team does not involve only the people under me. It also involves the people above
that feed me with stuff and that helped me get better. The hair story here has been a success
and it's been a success because we're working together and that's the only reason. I wouldn't be
here talking or doing anything. I wouldn't have been a citizen backstage without any of them. So
that's very clear to me. We are now through a moment that we can create any hairstyle that we want
and I'm very proud of that. And with more than 30 new hair styles scheduled to make their way into
the persistent universe across each remaining patch this year, the options for self-expression
and Star Citizen are just one more way 2025 will continue to deliver more content than ever before.
Now, I also want to tell you about this new Squadron 42 spotlight that's being delivered
directly to inboxes right now about every two months or so. It comes with timed exclusives,
never before seen visuals, audio files, story information, all that kind of stuff included.
So don't forget to check your inboxes for that and then of course opt in through the
account settings on the website if you really want that content before everyone else. And then of
course for those of you with friends, nobody here. With friends thinking about trying out Star Citizen,
our very first free fly of the year starts today with six vehicles to choose from.
The universe truly is better with friends. For Star Citizen, I'm Jared Huckabee. As always,
thanks for letting us share the people and process of game development with you and we'll see you
all here next week. Let's wrestle when you begin.
